items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: That led to Shelly‟s group, because Shelly hired Conte and Vinnegar and me to be in his band.

ctx.x: Pete was – he had a really outgoing personality. When he moved to L.A., he wanted to have a band. He wanted to be an actor. He wanted to – I don‟t know whether he wanted to sing or not, but he wanted to do everything showbiz-related. Conte, he wasn‟t bashful, but he had a lower temperature personality, no Superman suit. But he was a wonderful player from the first time I heard him. He sounded like a much older guy in his ability to play jazz. I first heard him, I think, when Chubby Jackson first took a band to…

steady job down here on Hollywood Boulevard for two months, which is kind of unheard of at that time, because things were starting to get tight music-wise at that time. I really had a good time playing in his band. He had Larance Marable on drums, Vinnegar again on bass, Carl Perkins on piano, me on tenor, and Conte on trumpet, really a good band. It started out with Larry Bunker on drums. Then Larance came in later. That led to Shelly‟s group, because Shelly hired Conte and Vinnegar and me to be in his band. He…

Some of the other members of the orchestra on this date, The Fabulous Bill Holman, include one of your reedmates, who seems to recur on several of your projects, Richie Kamuca. Did I pronounce that correctly?

items.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: a lot of people left, Bob Cooper and Bud Shank and Shelly Manne and Shorty Rogers, a lot of the stars left

ctx.x: Were you on the band when he had the — didn’t he have a string section for a while?

Yeah. I think they called that the “Innovations in Modern Jazz” or something, so they called it the Innovations Orchestra. That was, he did two tours with that, I think in ’48 and ’49. That was before me. Then in 1951, at the end of 1951, a lot of people left, Bob Cooper and Bud Shank and Shelly Manne and Shorty Rogers, a lot of the stars left. So when he reorganized the band in early ’52 that’s when I joined. But no strings.
He certainly generates discussion about where he fits in jazz history. How do you feel about his place?
